en: “As a process of classification and social differentiation, in which objects/signs are ordered not only as significant differences within a code, but as status values within a hierarchy. In this sense, consumption may be the object of a strategic analysis that determines its specific weight in the distribution of status values (with the implication of other social signifiers: knowledge, power, culture, etc.) […] The principle of the analysis is the following: one never consumes the object in itself (in its use value) - objects (in the broad sense) are always manipulated as signs that distinguish the individual, either by affiliating him with his own group taken as an ideal reference or by setting him apart from that group by reference to a group of higher status. However, the process of status differentiation, which appears as the fundamental social process through which each person takes his place in society, presents a lived aspect and a structural aspect; one conscious and the other unconscious; one ethical (it is the morality of ‘standing’, of status competition and of the scale of prestige), the other structural - inscription in a code whose rules and constraints of signification […] essentially escape individuals. The consumer experiences his distinctive conduct as freedom […] and not as a constraint of differentiation and of obedience to a code. To differentiate oneself always amounts to establishing the total order of differences, which constitutes, without more, the fact of total society and inescapably goes beyond the individual. By distinguishing himself in the order of differences, the individual restores it, condemning himself, therefore, to inscribe himself in it only in a relative way. Each individual experiences his own differential social gains as absolute gains, and not the structural constraint that lies at the origin of the exchange of positions and of the permanence of the order of differences. Yet it is this constraint of relativity that is decisive, insofar as it is by reference to it that differential inscription will never come to an end. It alone explains the fundamental character of consumption, its UNLIMITED character - a dimension that cannot be explained by a theory of needs and satisfaction since, if it were calculated in caloric or energy balance or in use value, the saturation threshold would quickly be reached. Now, the truth is that we witness precisely the opposite - the acceleration of the rhythms of consumption, the ‘forcing’ of demand that opens the gap between a gigantic productivity and an even more frenzied consumptibility […] This fact has no explanation unless one radically abandons the individual logic of satisfaction in order to restore to the logic […] of differentiation its decisive importance. Or else, by distinguishing the logic of difference from the simple […] conscious determinations of prestige, which are still satisfactions, consumption of positive differences, whereas the distinctive sign proves to be at once positive and negative difference - a fact that leads it to refer indefinitely to other signs and to induce definitive dissatisfaction in the consumer.” <1>Baudrillard</1><2>(Baudrillard, 1995, p. 60- 61)</2>. <3>↩</3>

It is important to set aside the reading according to which the game, because it is free-to-play, that is, free to play, offers all characters natively to the user. Riot is clear in specifying that the currency “Blue Essence” (Essência Azul), earned through the expenditure of time and progress in missions internal to the game, can be used to obtain champions from shards (consumable items obtained through missions) or, through a greater expenditure of resources, to buy them directly in the store. This means that the playable champion is also treated as acquirable content and not as an automatically available element <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025o)</2>. <3>↩</3>

In the same official material, Riot defines RP as a premium currency “only obtainable through direct purchase in the store [...]”, that is, obtained by direct purchase <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025o)</2>. In addition, Riot maintains an institutional view of champion pricing, explaining that prices are set by criteria such as release date and difficulty level, which reinforces the existence of a pricing policy for this asset <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2025i)</4>. <5>↩</5>

The permanence of the “champion” in the account may coexist, by contractual design, with a broad elasticity of the properties that make up its enjoyment. In the <1>Champion Roadmap: January 2018</1>, Riot confirms that the champion Aatrox was about to receive the “largest pure gameplay update we’ve ever done” and that he needed to be “rethought from the ground <2>Riot Games</2><3>(Riot Games, 2018c)</3>. This is the core of nominal restoration, given that the very administrator of the sign admits the structural replacement of the functional content without this being presented as a replacement of the object, because the name and the discourse about belonging remain intact. <4>↩</4>

The analogy with volleyball is not meant to suggest that this is “another game”, but precisely the opposite: it preserves the crucial point that the sport remains the same, while the function and the regime of participation are replaced. In volleyball, even though everyone shares the same court and the same objective, the functions are not interchangeable without loss, because each involves a distinct set of technical skills, competences and expectations. The outside hitter is trained and valued to turn the ball into a point against the block, alternating power and direction, reading the opposing block and deciding in fractions of a second under conditions of high variability. The libero, by contrast, is specialized in defense and reception, focused on the stability of the first ball, on reading trajectory, positioning and coverage, and, by rule, does not even take part in the attack as the others do. The switch, therefore, is not merely “changing places”. It is a reprogramming of what counts as performance, of which technical gestures make sense and of which form of participation gives the way in which the merely formal continuity of the “same player on the roster” may coexist with the practical replacement of what was bought as a way of playing and of recognizing oneself in the enjoyment of the object. <1>↩</1>

In a compilation of developer discussions about the <1>rework</1> of the <2>juggernauts</2>, the direct formulation appears: “Candidly, Mordekaiser is pretty ‘forced’”, in the context of the debate about <3>melee bot lanes </3>and about the level of <4>pushing</4> that should come from the <5>design</5> itself <6>MOOBEAT</6><7>(Moobeat, 2015)</7>, establishing on an empirical record the thesis that nominal restoration has the potential to include institutional migration of function and of mode of enjoyment, something that does not arise as an accident but as a policy acknowledged in the very language of the backstage. <8>↩</8>

This is the controversy concerning the presence of short-range characters in the position of the lower lane (hence <1>bottom </1>or <2>bot lane</2>) of the geographic setting where matches take place. The same happens with the magic word, with simulation models and with advertising which, among other modes of discourse, preferably makes use of tautological discourse. Everything in it is ‘metaphor’> of one and the same thing: the brand. The expressions - ‘better beer’ (compared to what?). ‘Lucky Strike’, ‘toasted cigarette’ (but they all are!) lead only to a whirling self-evidence. When Hertz (‘the world’s no. 1 in car rental’) says at the end of a long advertisement: ‘Let us be logical. If you did not find something more with us, we would never have reached the position we hold… And perhaps others would be presenting this advertisement> - is this not pure tautology and proof by existence? It is repetition that everywhere gives rise to effective causality. Just as in certain laboratories the artificial synthesis of molecules is carried out, here too the ‘artificial synthesis’ of the true is performed out of the efficient word. ‘Persil-washes-whiter> is not a sentence, but the Persil discourse. This and other advertising syntagms do not explain, do not provide any meaning, are neither true nor false - but they eliminate precisely meaning and proof. They replace it with an indicative without sentences, which is a repetitive imperative. This tautology of discourse seeks, as in the magic word, to induce tautological repetition through the event. The consumer, by means of the purchase, will merely consecrate the event of the myth.“ <1>Baudrillard</1><2>(Baudrillard, 1991, p. 135-136)</2>. <3>↩</3>

<1>Hypercuratorial anticipation</1>

On platforms, the IOC exists as an offer whose economic form depends on shared reading, public ranking and recognition within a circuit, capable of keeping value in circulation even when enjoyment shifts. From here on, the decisive axis becomes time as a governed dimension, because, in <1>games-as-a-service</1> regimes and continuous digital services, the promise of the IOC no longer behaves as a one-off delivery event and presents itself as administered continuity, in which value is sustained only by rhythms and milestones that the platform itself organizes.

Hypercuratorial anticipation designates an economic-semiological technique by which the platform produces a consumable future through continuous curation, defining what will come, what will disappear, what will return and what will be raised to the status of an “event”. This production governs value itself by deciding rhythms, relevances and expectations within the ecosystem, converting calendar and presentation into instruments of legible distinction and relative measurement. It is the governance “of what is to come” as an operative part of the offer, with the <1>p. 314</1> administered future serving as an economic resource and as a device for steering conduct in the present.

The economic functioning of this regime can be described as the deliberate maintenance of continuous readiness. The consumer is kept in continuous readiness for “the next cycle”, “the next update”, “the next opportunity”, that is, for the next piece of meaning that reorders the positional value of the ecosystem. The present ceases to be the place of a stabilized delivery and becomes a governed antechamber, in which the promise is renewed through announcements, <1>teasers</1><2><3>356</3></2>, <4>roadmaps</4><5><6>357</6></5> and “seasons” that function as advance delivery in the sphere of recognition. Thus, the platform does not sell only the “now”, since it also sells permanence oriented toward the “to come”, converting expectation into an asset and turning waiting into a material component of enjoyment.

This technique can be seen clearly when the company itself publicly structures the “to come” as a communicable object, in layers and in the language of promise, forming an administered horizon of announcements, corrections and returns. Rather than appearing as the consumer's mere expectation, the future is produced as an institutional calendar and as a repertoire of signals, with release windows, schedule forecasts, teasers and updates that become, in practice, part of what sustains permanence and decision. In this register, development updates function as explicit management of the “to come”, by presenting what is being prepared for the year and by condensing announcements into a sequence, with time frames, forecasts and references to longer pieces of context <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024q)</2><3><4>358</4></3>. The promise is thus not limited to “having something new”, because it is organized as direction, agenda and milestones of attention, so that the consumer's presence comes to be oriented by a series of imminences.

<1>p. 315</1> This serialization becomes even more tangible when the competitive design is reconfigured as a program of stages. By announcing and justifying three splits in each ranked season, the company converts the year into smaller units of participation, with rewards and tracks tied to the completion of these units <2>Riot Games</2><3>(Riot Games, 2024h)</3><4><5>359</5></4>. As a result, enjoyment no longer refers only to access to the game and comes to depend on showing up for windows, on completing cycles and on remaining in cadences that the ecosystem makes operative so that positional value does not degrade. The institutional insistence on continuity throughout the season and on consistency in each split frames time as organizable raw material, not as a neutral background.

The government of time gains precision when temporalization is converted into executable dates and times, as in the patch notes that announce the end of one split and the beginning of another with time stamps and a reference to the local time zone, turning “missing a window” into an administratively delimited event <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024o)</2><3><4>360</4></3>. What theoretical discourse describes as continuous readiness here appears as practical infrastructure. The cycle expires on a set day and time and restarts at another, so that the consumer's permanence in the circuit is calibrated by an official regime of deadlines that disciplines return, intensifies urgency and reorganizes the meaning of “being up to date”.

This design, in turn, does not lack institutional backing, for the contract frames instability as governable normality and recognizes as legitimate the reprogramming of content, access and rhythm by unilateral decision, including through updates and modifications that may occur with or without notice <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. The “consumable future” becomes economically relevant because the promise need not be fulfilled in full as stable delivery, it is enough that it remain credible and mobilizing, while the operability of the ecosystem is preserved by signals and calendars that the platform itself administers. Anticipation, in this sense, ceases to be mere persuasion and comes to function as a technique of value capture, since it turns waiting into economically oriented conduct and makes permanence a practical response to the risk of expiration.

<1>p. 316</1> The immediate economic effect is the replacement of a logic “of delivery” by a logic “of directed trajectory”. The promise is always reframed as a succession of stages, events and returns, so that enjoyment becomes structurally incomplete without the next cycle. The future need not be realized in full; it is enough that it remain credible and mobilizing. Delivery can thus be continually postponed without appearing as failure, because the system keeps the user in motion, rewarding adherence with sufficient signals of continuity and with calibrated temporal scarcity. Hypercuratorial anticipation, in this sense, is not a <2>marketing</2> ornament, but a technique for governing time that monetizes expectation as a regular means of maintaining value.

This anticipation is economically relevant for IOCs because it sustains the conversion of expectation into present value, altering the very logic of the consumer's decision and permanence. When acquiring an immaterial good in this regime, one adheres not merely to an isolated item, but to a place within a governed flow, in which what “has value” is also the capacity to continue to count in the ecosystem as the calendar unfolds. As a result, price, urgency and convenience come to incorporate the to come as a component of evaluation, since the consumer's situation comes to be measured by access to cycles, by presence at temporal milestones and by permanence on a public scale that is continually updated.

When time is governed in this way, it ceases to be a background and becomes an instrument of command, because the platform comes to produce not only content, but administered instability. Predictability, which in traditional consumption functions as a minimum condition for planning and comparison, is replaced by a regime in which rhythms, returns, disappearances and reclassifications are continually reprogrammable, and this reprogramming operates as a technique for steering conduct in the present. The practical effect is not only the intensification of desire or urgency, but the compression of the space of agency of the consumer, who loses the capacity to orient conduct, anticipate consequences and stabilize legitimate expectations about the permanence of what was promised. In this key, the “to come” becomes a functional component of the immaterial good and a sensitive point of verifiability, because shifts in the calendar and in presentation may produce relevant losses without a single, easily identifiable event of non-performance.

An operational analogy helps make the concept more concrete. In an urban transit subscription plan, the value lies not only in the card acquired, but in the stability of the system that makes it usable, lines, schedules, transfers and access rules. If the operator, without formally breaching the contract, begins to change schedules frequently, eliminate transfers, reclassify routes and introduce variable validation obstacles, the <1>p. 317</1> consumer may continue “having access to the service”, but loses the capacity to plan trips and to foresee practical consequences, which affects the adequacy of the service as a continuous regime. In platform consumption, hypercuratorial anticipation works in a similar way, only with calendars, progression milestones, promises of return and public forms of visibility that are reprogrammed as part of governance. The point is that the strategic mutability of the to come reconfigures, in the present, the space of agency and the minimum stability of legitimate expectations that make up the value of the IOC.

This curated future materially integrates the offer and materializes through a recurring set of devices that organize consumption as flow. The “to come” ceases to be a simple subjective expectation and becomes part of what is put into circulation, because the platform sells the promise of access to sequences, milestones and returns as if they were properties of the good itself, capable of generating socially effective recognition already in the present. In this regime, the IOC is not only what one obtains now, but also what one is authorized to expect and to claim as probable continuity within the ecosystem, which shifts the offer to a model in which the calendar and the presentation of the to come function as operative components of value.

These devices are recurring and recognizable. Seasons and <1>roadmaps</1> structure expectation as a horizon in chapters, converting continuity into meaning and relevance. Passes and progression tracks condition presence and return by tying value to goals and temporal milestones. Events and collections fabricate belonging and public memory by transforming acquisition into situated participation. Availability windows produce temporal scarcity by making access a problem of <2>timing</2>, and not only of price. Returns and relaunches recalibrate prestige by reorganizing what counts as rare, current or “back”. Editions and variations establish an internal scale by grading differences and transforming nuances into legible hierarchy.

With these devices, the promise is no longer structured as closed delivery and comes to operate as a serialized promise, in which the sequence becomes the relevant economic unit. What is bought is not only a result, but the maintenance of a circuit that unfolds through stages, updates and planned returns, so that “delivering” comes to mean sustaining the operability of value over time. The offer is thus reorganized as administered continuity, because the immaterial good remains economically active insofar as it is reinscribed in cadences and milestones that reactivate expectation, renew comparison and preserve the consumer's position within the flow.

<1>p. 318</1> When the promise is serialized and the sequence constitutes the economic unit, adequacy comes to depend on the good remaining operative in the circuit that gives it value, that is, continuing to be recognizable, measurable and socially confirmable in the ecosystem throughout the governed cadences. In this regime, the relevant delivery is not measured only by residual access, but by the practical preservation of the position of enjoyment within a flow in which value and recognition are updated over time.

At this point, expectation ceases to be a psychological by-product of consumption and comes to function as produced infrastructure, because the platform fabricates, administers and distributes the state of “almost delivery” as the regular mode of existence of the promise. Anticipation does not appear as an empty interval between purchases, but as an operative track that sustains interest, an internal scale of value and social insertion while the object has not yet been realized, or even when it is never realized in a fully stable way. The ecosystem organizes waiting as a governed experience, in which signals of the future, milestones and announcements function as material elements of the circuit, keeping value active through the continually reactivated promise.

Structured as a track, it is converted into routine through cycles of participation, goals and milestones that demand recurring presence for the position to remain operative. Tasks, progressions, <1>checkpoints</1> and temporal rewards transform enjoyment into conduct, because value comes to depend on completing stages and keeping up with the rhythm imposed by the ecosystem, and not only on “having” an item. Conduct, in turn, is converted into permanence, since returning ceases to be a neutral choice and becomes a practical condition for not losing sequence, not losing access to milestones and not losing the continuity of the public recognition that sustains the acquired position.

The urgency produced by this regime is not diffuse emotion, because it operates as the administration of the risk of losing one's place in a legible hierarchy. Missing a window, failing a milestone or ignoring a cycle is not equivalent to “missing a chance”, but to dropping in position in the public regime of comparison that the ecosystem updates in real time. Time is instrumentalized to convert absence into visible disadvantage, so that “being left out” means positional demotion and a socially observable loss of relevance. Decision and permanence are thus driven by structured risk, not by spontaneous affect.

This temporal regime only works because it is coupled to a regime of visibility that converts time into public distinction. The calendar does not organize only access and opportunity, for it transforms dated participation into a displayable mark of being current, belonging and prestige, making being up to date a comparable differential. Time, scene and position operate as one and the same mechanism, insofar as the curation of the to come defines what <1>p. 319</1> matters, public exposure turns this into a criterion of hierarchy and the consumer's position remains operative only while it receives continuous social validation. Anticipation, here, is not an internal rhythm of the service, but a mechanism of exposed stratification.

In this key, governed time takes the form of a continuous present produced by flow, in which novelties and repositionings replace one another without allowing interpretive rest. What matters is always the now that expires, and the continuity of the experience rests less on the stability of the object than on the obligation to keep up with what has been made relevant. Attention is maintained by recurrence, and permanence is normalized as a practical response to an environment that ceaselessly redefines what must be seen, compared and pursued.

Likewise, signals of the future function as symbolic equivalences sufficient to sustain adherence and conduct, even if enjoyment is unstable, degradable or reconfigurable. Promises of return, of appreciation, of an imminent event or of a next phase operate as anticipated delivery on the plane of social validity, for they keep the circuit active through expectation and commensurability even when the concrete referent has not yet been realized or has already been altered. The ecosystem comes to operate through promises that are worth something in themselves in everyday practice, insofar as the announced to come becomes part of what is bought, of what is justified and of what is accepted as continuity of value.

When the offer takes the form of a temporal program, the link between promise and delivery can no longer be verified by simple inspection, because it comes to depend on continuous decisions that do not present themselves as fixed “content” of the item. Curation of rhythm, selection of what appears and what disappears, relevance criteria, regimes of visibility, comparison parameters and repositioning rules operate as structural layers of delivery and can be recalibrated without an identifiable event of rupture. Opacity, therefore, is neither communication noise nor a lack of attention on the consumer's part: it is the effect of a reconfigurable architecture in which what is at stake is the maintenance of the conditions that keep the promise holding over time.

In this scenario, trust migrates from the item to the ecosystem that makes it operative, because what matters is not only access, but the continuity of the public validity of the acquired position. The expectation of stability comes to fall on the platform as the private guarantor of the circuit: the instance that will preserve cadences, relevances and the parameters of measurement and endorsement by which the acquisition made sense. Delivery, in practice, is experienced as the institutional stability of the environment, and not as the objective permanence of an isolated object, which makes the consumer dependent on the continuous governance of the very system that defines what has value, what appears and what continues to count as “the same”.

<1>p. 320</1> The teleology of extraction is reinforced because hypercuratorial anticipation monetizes recurrence: it converts time and attention into the raw material of value and turns permanence into an economic input. By serializing the promise and treating the to come as an operative component of the offer, the platform shifts the center of monetization to repetition, return and the maintenance of presence in cadences that it administers itself. Consumption ceases to be an event and becomes a regime, in which the continuous governance of the ecosystem is the condition for extraction to be effective.

The sensitive point is that this same ecosystem may preserve labels, signals and public commensurability while shifting, from within, the real conditions of the position of enjoyment. Anticipation facilitates this exchange because the future promise functions as a buffer: the announced to come takes the place of the present loss and sustains the sense of continuity even when restrictions, practical effects, modes of access or performance conditions change in a relevant way. Thus, restoration may operate as a socially legible nominal equivalence, preserving prestige, belonging and comparability, while the experience that justified that position is degraded or reconfigured without a clear marker of rupture.

If the value of the IOC depends on controlled semiosis, on administered visibility, on operative symbolic equivalences and on time governed as a program, then the central problem ceases to be only the content of the item and comes to be the demonstrability of the link between promise and enjoyment in a reconfigurable environment. The consequence is that the relevant exposure is not only informational, for it falls on the possibility of proving what sustained the promise at the moment of acquisition and what was altered in the experience over time. This is what requires naming and delimiting semiotic vulnerability as a structural loss of verifiability when experience and value are produced by regimes of signs, of scene and of calendar unilaterally controlled by the platform.

They designate short pieces of anticipatory communication, generally fragmentary or enigmatic, aimed at arousing curiosity and building expectation around future releases or updates. In the IOC regime, they function as instruments of "hypercuratorial anticipation", organizing the consumer's horizon of desire and preparing their economic conduct before the promised utility is actually made available. <1>↩</1>

“<1>Roadmap</1>” is an expression used in the sense of public (or semi-public) planning of the evolution of the service. It is the narrative of priorities, deliveries and future milestones, used both for internal coordination and for managing external expectations. Translations such as “roteiro” or “plano” are more generic and do not capture the communicational character typical of the term in the context of platforms (promise, signaling of direction, justification of delays and reorganizations). Therefore, “<2>roadmap” </2>is used because it is the standard label of the sector's own informational regime. <3>↩</3>

In a development communication about the 2024 Season, Riot presents the very idea of the future as an object of editorial management, by declaring that it will bring together people “from all of Riot” to talk about what is being prepared for 2024 and by promising a “brief summary” with announcements, in addition to referring the reader to longer texts. The form matters because it organizes the “to come” as an official sequence of items, offering direction and continuity as part of the value of remaining attentive to the ecosystem <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024q)</2>. <3>↩</3>

In the development text about ranked rewards, the temporal cut appears as the avowed architecture of the year, by stating that there are three splits in each ranked season and by linking the incentive to keep playing to a consistency distributed across these splits. The practical consequence is that positional progress is coupled to smaller cycles and that absence is converted into lost opportunity within a previously delimited window <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024h)</2>. <3>↩</3>

The notes for Patch 14.18 make explicit the executable character of the window by fixing the end and beginning of the splits with date and time, converting the split into an objective temporal boundary. In this logic, time ceases to be mere context and comes to operate as an institutionally marked condition of enjoyment, for the cadence imposes itself as an official calendar of expiration and restart <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024o)</2>. <3>↩</3>

<1>Semiotic vulnerability</1>

Under the regime described, the good is not sustained as an isolated “thing”, but as a position of enjoyment dependent on intelligibility, comparison and recognition in a governed ecosystem. The structural consequence of the regime described is to observe consumption through the prism of delivery and proof, for the relevant exposure takes the form of a loss of verifiability of the link between promise and enjoyment in a governed ecosystem. In this environment, adjustments of visibility, relevance criteria, calendar rhythms and signals of prestige may alter, without an evident marker, what sustains the position of enjoyment as valuable. The center of the <1>p. 321</1> problem is the practical difficulty of demonstrating what was promised as position and what remained as delivery when the conditions of value are administered as a flow.

Semiotic vulnerability designates the consumer's structural exposure to the platform's unilateral control of the conditions that make the promise hold as delivery when the good is a position of enjoyment and not an autonomous thing. It appears when intelligibility, visibility, equivalence and temporal cadence cease to be background and come to make up the very mode of existence of the object, so that value depends on codes of reading, on public hierarchies, on markers of recognition and on rhythms that the environment continually administers. For this reason, the core lies not in ignorance of a clause or in an information deficit, but in the loss of the capacity to verify and demonstrate the link between promise and enjoyment in a governed ecosystem, in which what counts as “delivery” can be shifted without clear notice and without a visible rupture of the object.

Nor is this vulnerability to be confused with a moral judgment of the consumer who “did not read” or “did not understand”, because the problem is not inattention to a text, but asymmetry over the bases that make the promise operative and over the possibility of reconstructing them with proof. Nor is it reducible to a psychologization of behavior, as if everything were explained by impulse, desire or “addiction”, since permanence is produced by an architecture of comparison and by the governance of time, and not by mere spontaneous affect. Nor is it an ornamental culturalism that treats signs as makeup over a neutral substance, because, in immaterial consumption, the symbolic is a material part of the offer when it defines recognition, commensurability and socially legible position. The point, in all cases, is structural, for it concerns the governance of the regime of signs, of scene and of time as a condition of value and as the source of a specific loss of verifiability.

When the good is positional, the everyday confirmation of delivery tends to shift from the promise-enjoyment link to a promise-signal link, because what the ecosystem makes visible and circulable as recognition comes to function as a practical criterion of fulfillment. Markers of rarity, belonging, prestige, being current, participation in an event and other labels stabilize the position as a legible and comparable difference. These signals may remain intact even when the relevant enjoyment has been degraded or reconfigured, maintaining the public appearance of continuity and making the loss harder to convert into rupture. This shift is the heart of the problem, because it transforms the conflict into a dispute about criteria and equivalences, and not only about “the item” itself.

<1>p. 322</1> Semiotic vulnerability does not result from an isolated asymmetry, for it derives from a matrix of layers that combine in the same ecosystem and reinforce the shift from promise-enjoyment to promise-signal. There is an asymmetry of meaning, linked to control over codes of reading, categories and classifications that define what counts as relevant difference. There is an asymmetry of visibility, linked to control over the field of what appears, what is highlighted and what becomes comparable as prestige. There is a temporal asymmetry, linked to control over cadences, windows and cycles that make value depend on continuous presence. And there is an evidentiary asymmetry, linked to control over records, metrics, versions and internal criteria that determine what can be demonstrated later.
These layers couple together as a mechanism and produce a structural loss of verifiability: the central problem is not only knowing, but being able to prove.

The layer of meaning operates when the platform governs the intelligibility of the good without needing to alter the item technically in any overt way, because reclassifying, recategorizing, renaming attributes and reordering repertoires alters what the object “is” for the ecosystem. An IOC may remain accessible and, even so, lose the status that made it economically operative. The rare becomes common, the distinctive becomes ordinary, the “event” item becomes noise, the signal of belonging becomes indifferent, the difference in <1>status</1> that justifies the acquisition is lost over an undisclosed period and without any notice. This kind of shift is not peripheral, because, in immaterial consumption, the identity of the good is partly constituted by this shared grammar that allows recognition, comparison and validation. When the platform controls this grammar and recalibrates it unilaterally, it also controls the semantic stability of the acquired position. For this reason, it is able to produce relevant losses without producing a clear event of “breakage” of the item.

An empirical case that makes this semantic instability explicit is the controversy surrounding the <2>Soul Fighter Samira</2> <1>skin</1>, released in the <4>Ultimate</4> <3>tier</3> in 2023<5><6>361</6></5>. The legally relevant point is not to discuss “taste” or to turn community criticism into a measure of truth, but to observe how the ecosystem itself comes to depend on a unilateral redefinition of what the sign of the <7>tier</7> promises. When the platform treats the <8>Ultimate</8> category as a label whose definition can be rewritten over time by more open criteria, it alters, through <9>p. 323</9> language and classification, what counts as delivery, without needing to admit any non-fulfillment of what was offered<10><11>362</11></10>.

The consumer, up to that point, was still faced with the label and the catalog's top price, but felt the loss of a stable standard of auditability of the promised content, because comparison ceases to rest on a historically verifiable technical repertoire and comes to depend on the institutional framing of what would be “special” for that champion. The practical effect is to shift verification outside the point of purchase and outside the supplier's self-description, producing a regime in which proof of the promise-enjoyment link becomes litigious, socially disputed and informationally costly, precisely because what was sold as a category comes to operate as an elastic sign administered by the supplier itself<1><2>363</2></1>.

The layer of visibility reinforces the mechanism because positional value depends on what can be exposed, compared and confirmed as relevant difference in a public circuit. The platform does not merely present an offer; it organizes the field of comparison by defining showcases, highlights, apparent metrics, orderings and display patterns that turn reputation and social proof into value infrastructure. Enjoyment, then, includes occupying a recognizable place before others, and the good also derives its value from the way it lets itself be seen, measured and validated. For this reason, permanence ceases to be a behavioral detail and comes to function as a practical condition for maintaining value: without return and presence in the flow, the position falls out of date, loses legibility and loses social effectiveness. Even without any technical alteration to the item, the mere reconfiguration of what appears, of how it appears and of what counts as relevant can demote or elevate the IOC, shifting the value of the position without necessarily generating a clear marker of non-performance.

The layer of equivalence manifests itself when the ecosystem is able to preserve the appearance of fulfillment through signals that keep the good commensurable and recognizable, even though the relevant enjoyment has been reconfigured from within. The platform preserves the label, class, frame of rarity, form of display and comparative place of the item, <1>p. 324</1> ensuring that it continues to “read” as equivalent in the internal hierarchies, while functions, restrictions, modes of access, performance conditions and practical effects may be altered, degraded or emptied. Value remains operative because the circuit of recognition keeps working. The good remains validatable as difference, even if the experience that justified that difference has changed. This does not depend on individual psychological deception, since it is a mode of operation in which equivalence is produced by internal criteria and by stable signals, capable of sustaining public continuity without necessarily preserving the position of enjoyment in its relevant elements.

The temporal layer closes the circuit when time is governed as a program and the promise ceases to behave as a one-off event, becoming the administered sequence typical of <1>games-as-a-service</1>. Seasons, passes, tracks, events, roadmaps, availability windows, returns and relaunches are not “extra content”, they are devices that organize relevance and access, convert expectation into present value and turn “being up to date” into a practical criterion of belonging and being current. Permanence becomes a requirement because the position remains operative only if the consumer keeps up with the cadences and milestones that the ecosystem imposes, and because the experience itself is anchored in continuous decisions about what appears, what disappears and what returns. This intensifies semiotic vulnerability by multiplying barely legible points of recalibration and by shifting delivery to a field of administered temporal choices, in which “maintaining value” depends on the rhythm and the framing that the platform governs.

When these layers operate together, permanence and recurrence cease to be a “side effect” attributable to individual habit and become the very economic form of immaterial consumption, because the position is worth something only while it remains validated in the ecosystem. Return becomes an input because the environment transforms recognition into a recurring task, transforms being current into a condition of belonging and transforms absence into a risk of visible demotion, so that repeating and remaining are not psychological excesses, but practical requirements for preserving socially operative value. The teleology of extraction stabilizes precisely when consumption ceases to be an episode and becomes a regime in which meaning, visibility, equivalence and time are governed to produce continuity as necessity, and not as preference.

The state of risk becomes palpable when the platform unilaterally alters the attributes that sustain a sign of value already incorporated as identity and as social position. The <1>nerf</1> is a prime example in this scenario, since it is not merely a neutral technical adjustment, but a reconfiguration of what counts as power, relevance and prestige within the <2>p. 325</2> ecosystem, carried out by whoever controls the “physics of the world” in the form of code. When an item, an ability, a character, a category or a status marker is rescaled, demoted or redefined, it is not only a performance that is altered. What is altered is the public meaning of the investment and, in many cases, the very intelligibility of the acquired position.

Symbolic debasement is relevant because it produces loss through mutation of the internal rule of value, and not through an overt functional failure. The consumer may continue to have “access” to the same nominal item, the same inventory and the same ownership marker, while losing, from within, the practical effects and the symbolic effects that made that position hold as delivery. Contestation becomes difficult because the platform does not break the object. It goes further, redefining the very world in which the object holds value. In evidentiary terms, rupture ceases to be an event and becomes a recalibration, and it is precisely this form of loss that demands parameters of traceability and of substantive equivalence, to prevent the mutation of the sign from functioning as a normalized path of demotion without demonstrable consequence.

Under these premises, the notion of adequacy cannot be decided by the binary “works/does not work”, because it is perfectly possible to maintain technical access and, even so, lose what made the position economically operative. If the relevant unit is position, circuit and sequence, adequate delivery depends on the good remaining recognizable, comparable and validatable on the terms that sustained its value in the ecosystem, and not only on continuing to be “present” as a nominal item in the inventory. Reading the good as a closed unit fails because it ignores that, in immaterial consumption, a decisive part of value is produced by governed conditions of intelligibility, visibility and cadence, which can be recalibrated without an identifiable event of rupture. For this reason, minimum functioning does not serve as a sufficient yardstick: it confuses technical continuity with preservation of the position of enjoyment that made the acquisition hold as delivery.

A typical risk of this regime is merely nominal restoration, in which label, category and public markers of continuity are preserved, while the conditions that constituted the position of enjoyment are altered from within. The platform keeps the good legible for the showcase and for social comparison, with declared rarity, frame of prestige, belonging and internal commensurability, and, at the same time, recalibrates access, restrictions, effects, performance conditions, modes of display and relevance criteria that sustained the acquired experience. Rupture is neutralized because the circuit of recognition continues to produce social proofs of delivery, even when the relevant content of enjoyment has been <1>p. 326</1> shifted. The result is a loss that tends to be absorbed as a normal adjustment of the ecosystem, for the continuity of the signal takes the place of the continuity of the position, which makes it difficult to transform internal reconfiguration into demonstrable non-performance.

For this reason, the relevant object of proof also changes. It is not enough to demonstrate that “the item exists” or that “access remains”. What must be capable of reconstruction are the conditions that sustained the promise at the moment of acquisition and that constituted the position of enjoyment as operative in the ecosystem, that is, which functions, restrictions, modes of access and parameters of recognition made that position valuable, comparable and validatable. The evidence required ceases to be mere inspection of the current state of the good and becomes reconstruction of the link: which classifications, metrics, visibility criteria, cadences, rules and equivalences were in force when the promise was assumed and how they were altered afterward. Without this change of focus, the dispute remains trapped on the surface of “appearing-as-delivery”, precisely where nominal continuity and public signals are most efficient at concealing relevant losses in enjoyment.

Auditability, in this context, is the minimum requirement of verifiability in a market in which delivery depends on opaque and adjustable layers. It means the possibility of reconstructing, in a traceable way, the conditions that made the promise hold as delivery at the moment of acquisition and the relevant alterations that affected those conditions over time, without depending on the self-validation produced by the platform itself. What must leave a trace is not a generic “trade secret”, but what is material to the acquired position of enjoyment, such as criteria for classifying and reading the item, parameters that organize visibility and comparison, rules and metrics that sustain recognition and belonging, and temporal decisions that shape access, cadence and relevance.

Without this minimum, the dispute tends to be resolved by surface and impression, because the continuity of signals functions as self-justifying proof while the consumer cannot demonstrate what changed, by which criteria and with what effect on the acquired position. Auditability, therefore, enters not as a regulatory luxury or a moralization of the symbolic, but as a practical condition for the promise-enjoyment link to be demonstrable in markets of continuous governance. Even so, tracing is not enough in itself: a criterion is also needed to judge whether what was preserved after the alteration corresponds, in fact, to the relevant value of the position, and it is precisely there that the requirement of functional value equivalence imposes itself.

Functional value equivalence is the criterion that prevents restoration from being reduced to continuity of name, label, declared rarity or public symptoms of <1>p. 327</1> “sameness” when what was acquired was a position of enjoyment. To be equivalent, here, does not mean to appear equivalent for the showcase, but to preserve, in a substantive way, the relevant elements that made that position hold as delivery, including practical functions, applicable restrictions, modes of access, performance conditions and effects that structured the acquired experience. Since, in the IOC, part of the value is materially produced by recognition and commensurability in the ecosystem, the “functional” also covers this component only insofar as it was an operative condition of the position bought, that is, that without which the good ceases to function as recognizable difference on the relevant terms of the acquisition. This does not authorize turning any symbolic value into an indeterminate legal obligation; on the contrary, it requires isolating what was relevant to that specific position and assessing whether the restoration preserved that core or merely maintained signals of continuity while shifting, from within, what mattered. The effect of the parameter is to separate legitimate adjustment from opportunistic substitution: if the system preserves appearance and label, but substantially demotes functions, restrictions, access, performance or the social operability that defined the position, there was nominal restoration and not preservation of delivery. Recomposition thus ceases to be arbitrated by the platform as “equivalent by declaration” and becomes controllable by a substantive yardstick, compatible with a reconfigurable market, but hostile to the zone of impunity of the sign.

These parameters do not target the symbolic, because the symbolic has already been recognized as a material part of the mode of existence of the IOC as a position of enjoyment in the ecosystem. The problem appears when the continuity of signals comes to function as a substitute for substantive preservation and as an evidentiary shortcut, allowing “appearing-as-delivery” to absorb internal demotions as if they were simple adjustments. Auditability confronts this risk by requiring demonstrable traceability of the conditions that sustain the promise and of the alterations that reconfigure it, reducing dependence on evidence produced by the circuit itself. Functional value equivalence confronts the same risk in content, by requiring that restoration preserve, in a verifiable way, the relevant elements of the acquired position, instead of maintaining only label and public commensurability. The result is not to deny signs, but to reduce the space in which the continuity of the signal replaces proof of delivery when the platform preserves appearance and shifts, from within, what made delivery hold.

Taken together, the mechanism closes as a single gear: administered semiosis makes the good intelligible and desirable as a position; hierarchized visibility turns comparison and social proof into value infrastructure; equivalence by signals allows the promise to remain operative even when the relevant enjoyment shifts; and governed <1>p. 328</1> time serializes the promise, making the to come an economic resource that converts permanence into a requirement. In this scenario, delivery is not reduced to technical access, and the conflict tends to concentrate on the verifiability of the link between promise and enjoyment, precisely because the environment can preserve signals of continuity while recalibrating the criteria and conditions that sustained the value of the acquired position.

A privileged way of visualizing this loss of verifiability is the <1>nerf</1>, understood as the technically deliberate weakening of attributes, abilities or items, by means of a patch, to make something less powerful in the practical functioning of the game <2>League of Legends Wiki</2><3>(League of Legends Wiki, [202-?]m)</3><4><5>364</5></4>. The operation appears as an “adjustment”, but its relevant consequence, from the perspective of the IOC, is the practical reclassification of what counts as power, efficiency and prestige. The platform preserves access and the continuity of the good's label, while demoting, from within, what made the position count as delivery, which shifts the core of enjoyment without necessarily producing a clear external marker that would allow the consumer to reconstruct the promise-enjoyment link.

This effect is neither collateral nor exceptional, for the contractual regime of the ecosystem itself incorporates the <1>nerf</1> as an ordinary power to govern the service, including over virtual products <2>Riot Games</2><3>(Riot Games, 2024e)</3><4><5>365</5></4>. At the same time, virtual content is qualified as a limited and revocable license, setting aside the language of ownership and reinforcing that permanence of access does not mean substantive preservation of the value enjoyed <6>Riot Games</6><7>(Riot Games, 2024e)</7><8><9>366</9></8>. The fit is methodologically revealing, since the <10>nerf</10> is not merely a <11>p. 329</11> numerical alteration, but a technique for administering the meaning of value that preserves the appearance of continuity while altering the functional content of the position, making it harder to demonstrate, in verifiable terms, what was actually lost.

The public language of balancing, in turn, tends to operate as a legitimizing narrative for this governance by continuous modulation. In the patch notes, the “nerfs” are presented as necessary corrections to keep the environment “healthy” and to stabilize experiences, while at the same time describing concrete reductions of power that reconfigure what counts as advantage, viability and performance <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2026d)</2><3><4>367</4></3>. The discourse produces intelligibility for the alteration and offers technical justification for the loss, but does not resolve the central problem. The question that matters is not whether the game can be adjusted, but under what conditions the platform can treat as “compatible with the promise” a substantive demotion of delivery<5><6>368</6></5>, when the very criterion of what counts as delivery remains under unilateral administration and with traces whose form and sufficiency are also defined by the same authority.

In this key, semiotic vulnerability ceases to look like a problem of “consumer sensitivity” and appears as a structural risk of a market in which equivalence can be proclaimed by signals. The <1>nerf</1> is the limit case because it shows, with precision, how the continuity of name and access can function as self-justifying proof<2><3>369</3></2>, while the relevant delivery shifts in what the environment counts as power and utility.

<1>p. 330</1> Semiotic vulnerability thus names this type of structural loss of demonstrability that occurs when meaning, scene, equivalence and time materially integrate what is put into circulation and remain under the unilateral administration of the ecosystem. The question ceases to be whether changes are possible and becomes under what conditions they can be treated as compatible with the promise and with the preservation of the relevant value. In reconfigurable markets, altering the catalog, reordering visibility, redesigning cycles and recalibrating signals make up the regular mode of governance, but this normality cannot function as a license to preserve continuity of appearance while the core of the position of enjoyment is shifted from within.

In /dev: State of Skins 2023, when announcing Samira's <1>Ultimate</1>, Riot began to state that the definition of <2>Ultimate</2> “has changed over the years” and that the goal becomes something like <3>best-in-class</3> and “truly special” for the champion, also admitting that the project had started as a <4>Legendary</4> and only later was elevated to <5>Ultimate</5>. The interest of the passage lies in the shift of the criterion of the <6>tier</6> to a standard that is less traceable and less auditable at the act of purchase, since the platform itself claims authority to rewrite the meaning of the label that organizes the consumer's legitimate expectation <7>Riot Games</7><8>(Riot Games, 2023c)</8>. <9>↩</9>

The public reaction to the case was structured precisely as a dispute over equivalence of delivery and over stability of meaning of the <1>tier</1>. A relevant part of the community criticism described the item as closer to a “Legendary+” than to an <2>Ultimate</2> by the historical standard, and specialized coverage recorded the central question as being whether the content would justify the framing and the price of an <3>Ultimate</3>. This matters less as “forum opinion” and more as a symptom that, when the definition of the tier becomes elastic, practical proof comes to depend on comparisons, <4>showcases</4> and external auditing of what was delivered in game <5>Ho · McIntyre</5><6>(Ho, 2023; McIntyre, 2023)</6>. <7>↩</7>

The institutional feedback cycle on the PBE itself shows how the platform tends to administer controversy through incremental adjustments and calibration of presentation, without acknowledging a structural deficit of equivalence of the tier. Thus, when conflict sets in on the plane of the sign, the supplier is still able to sustain the appearance of performance by maintaining the label and through public signals of “response”, while the discussion about what “delivery” would be becomes, itself, governed matter <1>BAGEL_SOCKS</1><2>(Bagel_Socks, [2023])</2>. <3>↩</3>

On the technical meaning of the term, the terminology entry records: “Nerf (Patch) [is] an official modification to the game which makes something less powerful; opposite of a buff.” <1>League of Legends Wiki</1><2>(League of Legends Wiki, [202-?]m)</2>. The formulation is useful because it shifts the <3>nerf</3> from a subjective impression to an operative category of the ecosystem itself, linked to an official modification that makes something “less powerful”, that is, that demotes power in comparable and measurable terms in the environment. As evidence of institutional use of the vocabulary, the patch notes mobilize expressions of weakening and descriptions of reduction of power as regular justifications of governance. In a recent example, one reads: “this nerf should ensure that her power wanes a bit.” <4>Riot Games</4><5>(Riot Games, 2026d)</5>. The note is important not because of the specific champion, but because of the structure of the statement. The platform names weakening as a legitimate instrument, attributes to it a corrective purpose and, with this, produces a layer of meaning that naturalizes the internal reconfiguration of value, regardless of its practical effects, opening room for the platform to use the same narrative for multiple purposes without allowing any questioning of its own assessment of the sustainability of the conditions of enjoyment in the environment. <6>↩</6>

The contract makes explicit the power of unilateral modulation of the service, including with the verb “nerf”. From this perspective, the <1>nerf</1> is not seen as a mere contingent event, but becomes part of the core of governance foreseen as the normality of the service, including over assets that, from the consumer's point of view, may have been acquired under symbolic promises of power and performance. <2>↩</2>

The qualification of virtual content as a limited license reinforces the structural asymmetry of the relationship and helps explain why restoration tends to be defended as “preservation of access” even when power has been demoted. The text is explicit: “what we are really offering you is a license and a personal right [...] revocable, limited” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. Mentioning the term does not serve to legitimize closing the analysis in favor of the platform, but to make visible the type of language that, in case of conflict, tries to absorb substantive losses as if they were internal variations without legal relevance, which aggravates the loss of verifiability of the promise-enjoyment link. <3>↩</3>

The public frame of balancing also leaves traces of how the platform understands the problem and which “levers” it is willing to pull. In an institutional response on the subject, it is stated that, as release approaches, “they’ll discuss the different levers they’re willing to pull if a champion releases too strong or too weak.” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2018b)</2>. The statement is valuable because it reveals balancing as a continuous practice of intervention through levers and not as a final state of equivalence, which resonates with the idea of governance by serial modulation and with the point that “stability” is, at most, a localized and negotiated objective, not a commitment verifiable by the consumer. <3>↩</3>

There are, moreover, public indications that certain champion designs generate cycles of intervention that make the very ideal of balance in the strong sense unstable, reinforcing the reading of balancing as management of variability, and not as preservation of equivalence. In coverage of a public statement attributed to the <1>designer </1>responsible for the champion <2>Zeri</2>, it is recorded: “Zeri is one of his greatest failures as a designer” and that she had been “nerfed into the ground” to avoid dominance in competitive play <3>Fisher</3><4>(Fisher, 2023)</4>. The statement does not present itself, in any instance, as conclusive proof. However, it shows that representatives of the ecosystem acknowledge, at least in certain cases, the structural tension between “working” at various levels of play and “remaining balanced” without interventions that significantly demote power for the user. <5>↩</5>

The hypothesis that balancing interventions may keep the door open to rent-seeking manipulation associated with the sale of cosmetics need not be treated as an accusation, but as a structural risk consistent with a model in which the environment is reconfigurable by design and the justifications for adjustment are produced by the very authority that alters the internal rule of value. Evidence that the suspicion is recurrent and even mobilizes attempts at empirical testing appears in a community analysis that declares: “To decide whether a champion got buffed when he gets a new skin, I will take the difference between the winrate 20 days before and 20 days after the patch got released.” <1>GIANTZORG</1><2>(giantZorg, 2019)</2>. The reference, shows that the very mode of governance by patches, added to the information asymmetry and to the absence of a clear duty of substantial equivalence, creates a zone in which suspicions of commercial optimization can thrive, precisely because the consumer does not have, as a rule, direct means to reconstruct and contest, with sufficient verifiability, the relationship between the promise of enjoyment and periodic reconfigurations of functional value. <3>↩</3>

The platform is an economic architecture, an arrangement that depends not only on price, but on permanence, repetition and continuous governance to extract value. Thus, the next step is to explain how this extraction becomes normalized and desirable in the consumer's experience, in a stable and recurring way. In immaterial consumption, capture is not sustained only by a clause or by a technical barrier. It is sustained by a regime of presentation, visibility and production of meaning that transforms choice into conduct and transforms enjoyment into permanence. For this reason, the description of the phenomenon must incorporate the semiotic dimension, since a decisive part of value is produced and stabilized in the way the offer presents itself, circulates and becomes recognizable as “delivery”.

In the field of IOCs, the object does not appear to the consumer as an isolated “thing”, nor as a simple accessed file. It appears as a position of enjoyment within a governed ecosystem, and this ecosystem already delivers the object wrapped in language, status and expectation. The offer, here, is always double, because it is composed of a narrative promise and an infrastructure of support. It is narrative because it presents meaning, rarity, belonging and prestige as if they were natural properties of the item. It is infrastructure because it exists only while the techno-media environment maintains the intelligibility of that meaning and the possibility of living it before others.

For this reason, the sign does not function as a communicational ornament of the product, but as a material component of the immaterial good itself. It is not a matter of an “image” superimposed on a neutral substance. It is a form of existence of the object, in which what is acquired is defined also by how it shows itself, by how it circulates and by how it can be recognized as valuable.

This mechanism acts in a practical and continuous way. The promise is not limited to the moment of purchase, nor is it exhausted in the formal description of the item. It operates as a script of conduct, because the signs that surround the IOC organize desire, urgency, comparison and belonging in real time. Enjoyment becomes, simultaneously, use and performance. The <1>p. 265</1> value of the good is not only what it “does”, but what it authorizes one to say about whoever holds it, where it places the subject within visible hierarchies and which symbolic doors it opens or closes within the community. Thus, identity, reputation and social integration cease to be side effects of consumption and come to make up the very circuit of the object. In this type of market, the platform governs not only the technical delivery of the good, but the symbolic conditions that make that delivery desirable, recognizable and continually renewed.

Under these conditions, the vulnerability that matters cannot be reduced to lack of information or to the old model of the consumer who “did not read” or “did not understand” the contract. The point is more structural. The consumer decides and remains within a field of meaning that he cannot audit, because the correspondence between the sign and the delivery depends on curations, metrics and continuous adjustments that are beyond his reach and, often, beyond even the formal text of the offer. The asymmetry lies not only in knowledge of clauses, but in the capacity to verify what really sustains the promise and under what conditions it can be altered, degraded or replaced without this appearing as an explicit breach. Hence the expression semiotic vulnerability. It is not a rhetorical adjective, but the name of a type of exposure in which the regime of signs governs experience and value, while the consumer's access to the bases of this governance is opaque, partial and reconfigurable.

If the regime of signs participates materially in the offer and in the very mode of existence of the IOC, legal control cannot be limited to examining formal declarations or to measuring harm as a simple failure of technical performance. The consequence is that the problem comes to require criteria of verifiability capable of reconstructing, with some degree of demonstrability, which conditions sustained the promise and how they operated in enjoyment. In this direction, auditability designates the requirement of traceability of the conditions that make the promise operative, allowing the link between expectation, architecture and experience to be reconstructed without depending only on the platform's self-description. Likewise, functional value equivalence designates the need to separate merely nominal restoration from effective preservation of the acquired position of enjoyment, since, in positionally defined goods, maintaining label and appearance may not preserve relevant functions, restrictions and effects. These names do not function as moralism against the symbolic, but as an anticipation of the type of control that will become necessary when the sign can operate as a shortcut of continuity and, with this, obscure proof of what was effectively delivered.

The semiotic block is organized as a tripod, but not as three contributions of the same weight and function. In Eco, the grammar of the problem is fixed, for the sign is treated as a structural and administrable component of intelligibility, an objective condition for the <1>p. 266</1> promise to exist socially and for the link between expectation and enjoyment to be reconstructed and demonstrated. In Debord, the mechanism is described by which this grammar is put into operation as a regime of visibility and comparison, making reputation, social proof and legible hierarchies part of the economic circuit of permanence. In Baudrillard, it is made explicit how equivalence can be stabilized by signals of delivery and by internal commensurability, allowing nominal restorations that preserve the public appearance of fulfillment without preserving the position of enjoyment in its relevant elements. The objective is not to multiply vulnerabilities by author, but to decompose, in layers, the conditions under which the governance of meaning is converted into governance of evidence and, with this, into a problem of verifiability amenable to protection by Law.
